name: Medulla: level of the pyramidal decussation
summary: The lowest transverse section of the brainstem, at the junction with the spinal cord, is dominated by the great motor decussation: most corticospinal fibers of each pyramid cross here to form the lateral corticospinal tract of the opposite side. The gray matter still looks spinal, with anterior and posterior horns, but the posterior columns are ending in the gracile and cuneate nuclei and the spinal trigeminal nucleus has replaced the substantia gelatinosa. A lesion here can produce the paradox of an arm weaker than the leg on opposite sides, because arm fibers cross higher than leg fibers.

anatomy.location: Just above the foramen magnum, from the first cervical root down to the point where the pyramids begin to bulge, roughly 35–45 mm below the anterior commissure in MNI coordinates (z ≈ −55 to −60).

subdivisions.name: Pyramidal decussation
subdivisions.note: corticospinal fibers crossing obliquely through the anterior median fissure into the contralateral lateral funiculus

subdivisions.name: Fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus
subdivisions.note: still present, capped by the beginnings of their nuclei

subdivisions.name: Spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract
subdivisions.note: lateral to the posterior horn, continuous with the substantia gelatinosa

subdivisions.name: Anterior horn cells
subdivisions.note: for the first cervical segment and the spinal accessory nucleus

subdivisions.name: Central canal
subdivisions.note: still central; it opens into the fourth ventricle at higher levels

function: Transition of the cord into the brainstem; the site where upper motor neuron control switches sides, which explains why lesions above this point give contralateral weakness and lesions below give ipsilateral weakness.

bestView.label: cervicomedullary junction: pyramids narrowing, decussating fibers crossing the midline
junction of medulla and cord above the foramen magnum

imaging.normalAppearance: On axial T2 the section is small and nearly round, with the pyramids as two anterior bulges and the posterior surface flat; gray matter is barely visible at 1 mm resolution. On sagittal images the level lies at the anterior lip of the foramen magnum.

pathology.pathology: Cervicomedullary compression (Chiari, basilar invagination, odontoid pannus)
pathology.finding: Indentation or kinking of the cervicomedullary junction by descended tonsils, the dens or rheumatoid pannus, sometimes with T2 signal change in the cord; cruciate paralysis or spastic quadriparesis.
Restricted diffusion in the ventral cervicomedullary junction from anterior spinal or vertebral artery disease.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T1/T2 and axial T2 through the craniocervical junction; flexion–extension CT for instability

lesionEffects.deficit: Cruciate paralysis: arm weakness with relatively spared legs
lesionEffects.mechanism: Arm fibers decussate more rostrally than leg fibers, so a lesion in the upper part of the decussation catches the arm fibers of both sides

lesionEffects.deficit: Hemiplegia cruciata: weakness of one arm and the opposite leg
lesionEffects.mechanism: A lesion at the level where arm fibers have crossed but leg fibers have not
Lesion caudal to the decussation after the fibers have crossed

examination: Compare proximal arm and leg power on both sides
Look for a Lhermitte sign and neck pain
Check lower cranial nerves to distinguish medullary from high cervical lesions
pearls: Arm-predominant quadriparesis after a craniocervical injury points to the pyramidal decussation
Below this level upper motor neuron lesions are ipsilateral; above it, contralateral
